alignment.note: Greek employs a participial construction (ὁ δὲ ἀποκριθείς ἔφη, 'and answering he said') with article and postpositive δέ; Peshitta uses simple ܐܡܪ ܠܗܘܢ ('he said to them'); Vulgate expands with Sed dico vobis ('But I say to you'), introducing a contrastive conjunction absent in the Greek and Peshitta.

Greek includes the particle μέν (G3303, 'indeed') to set up a contrastive structure anticipating a following δέ-clause; neither Peshitta nor Vulgate transmit this particle. Vulgate inserts quia et ('that also'), altering the syntactic frame to a subordinate clause rather than the Greek's main-clause assertion.

Greek and Peshitta preserve the rhetorical question about the Son of Man's suffering (πῶς γέγραπται... ἵνα πολλὰ πάθῃ, 'how is it written... that he should suffer many things'; Syriac ܘܐܝܟܢܐ ܟܬܝܒ... ܕܣܓܝ ܢܚܫ). Vulgate substitutes an entirely different clause: et fecerunt illi quæcumque voluerunt, sicut scriptum est de eo ('and they did to him whatever they wished, as it is written of him'), shifting focus from the Son of Man's prophesied suffering to Elijah's mistreatment, likely harmonising toward Matthew 17:12.
